ai.definition: General-purpose humanoids are bipedal robots designed to perform a wide range of physical tasks in various environments, mimicking human-like movements and interactions.
ai.howItWorks: These robots utilize advanced vision-language-action (VLA) models that enable them to understand visual inputs, process natural language commands, and execute corresponding actions. This integration allows for flexible task execution across different scenarios.
ai.problemSolved: They address the need for versatile automation in industries where human labor is required but may be costly or difficult to deploy due to safety concerns or physical constraints.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing general-purpose humanoids involves complex assembly processes, including the integration of sophisticated sensors, actuators, and AI systems. The production requires high precision and quality control measures.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the robotic structure, integrating hardware components like motors and sensors, programming VLA models for task execution, and conducting rigorous testing to ensure reliability and safety.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include advanced sensor technology, AI model development, and high-precision manufacturing processes. The complexity of integrating multiple technologies increases overall production costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook suggests that general-purpose humanoids are poised to enter the market in the near future, with early adopters likely coming from industries such as healthcare and logistics.
ai.regulation: Regulations will need to be developed to address safety standards, data privacy, and ethical considerations. Current regulatory frameworks may not fully cover these robots, necessitating new guidelines.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges in achieving human-like dexterity and perception, potential job displacement concerns, and the need for robust cybersecurity measures to protect against unauthorized access or manipulation.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain at this stage due to high initial costs and limited market penetration. However, as technology matures and adoption increases, profitability could become more feasible in specific niches.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving AI capabilities, enhancing physical robustness, and expanding the range of tasks these robots can perform autonomously or semi-autonomously.

glossary.def: AI systems that enable robots to understand visual inputs and process natural language commands for task execution.
Robots with two legs designed to walk, run, or perform tasks in a manner similar to humans.

subsystems.name: Actuated joints
subsystems.role: move each limb with enough torque and speed to handle real loads.

subsystems.name: Structure
subsystems.role: a light, stiff body that keeps the mass low enough to walk and carry.

subsystems.name: Hands and end effectors
subsystems.role: grasp and manipulate objects of unknown shape.

subsystems.name: Perception
subsystems.role: build a picture of the surroundings and the robot's own body.

subsystems.name: Onboard compute
subsystems.role: run the control neural network in real time.

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: carry enough energy for a useful working period.

subsystems.name: Control policy
subsystems.role: the learned software that turns goals and sensor data into joint commands.

buildSteps.title: Set the requirements
buildSteps.detail: Decide what the robot must lift, reach and how long it must run; this fixes limb lengths, joint torques and battery size.

buildSteps.title: Build the actuators
buildSteps.detail: Brushless motors are wound, geared down with harmonic or planetary reducers, fitted with torque sensors and driver electronics, then bench-tested for torque and heat.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the frame
buildSteps.detail: Limb links and the torso are machined or moulded from aluminium and carbon fibre, keeping mass down and stiffness up.

buildSteps.title: Wire and power it
buildSteps.detail: Battery pack, harnesses, cooling and emergency-stop circuits are routed through the joints without snagging.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Joints are fitted, encoders zeroed, and each actuator characterised so the controller knows its real behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Train the control policy
buildSteps.detail: Millions of simulated trials with randomised physics teach walking and manipulation; human teleoperation footage fine-tunes the harder hand skills.

buildSteps.title: Test safely
buildSteps.detail: The robot is run behind barriers and with a tether or gantry before working near people.

buildSteps.title: Pilot in a real workplace
buildSteps.detail: It performs one repetitive task, such as moving containers, under human supervision, while failures are logged and fixed.

prerequisites.why: electric joints must be strong enough to lift loads yet light enough to be carried by the robot itself.
training in simulation is the only practical way to learn balance and whole-body control.
runtime is measured in hours rather than full shifts, so most deployments need charging breaks.
grasping unfamiliar objects without crushing or dropping them remains unreliable.
rules for robots working beside people are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: pilots moving containers in warehouses and logistics sites, usually one task per robot, often with a human supervising several machines
pathway.unlocks: real operating data and evidence on reliability.

pathway.milestone: multi-task reliability over a full shift
pathway.unlocks: a robot that can be reassigned between jobs instead of retrained for one.

pathway.milestone: one operator supervising many robots remotely
pathway.unlocks: labour economics where a person directs a small fleet rather than one machine.

pathway.milestone: use in homes and small businesses
pathway.unlocks: help with chores and care tasks in places built for human bodies.

pathway.milestone: general-purpose manipulation that transfers between settings
pathway.unlocks: robots that learn new tasks quickly rather than being programmed per task.
